key_terms.meaning: An object whose value cannot change after creation; strings and tuples are immutable, lists are not.
Position number of an item in a sequence; s[0] is the first character and s[-1] is the last.
s[start:stop:step] returns a new sequence holding items from start up to but not including stop.
A function attached to a string object, called as s.method(), for example s.upper() or s.find('a').
A literal that starts with the letter f, where every {expression} inside the braces is replaced by its value.
The integer Unicode value of a character; ord(c) gives it and chr(n) reverses it.
s.split(sep) breaks one string into a list of strings at each sep; with no argument it splits on runs of whitespace.
sep.join(parts) glues a list of strings into one string, placing sep between neighbours.
s.strip() removes whitespace from both ends; s.strip(chars) removes any characters found in that string.
Mutable ordered sequence written [a, b, c]; items can be added, removed or replaced in place.
Two names bound to the same object, so a change made through one is seen through the other.
lst[:], list(lst) or lst.copy() makes a new outer list that still shares the inner item objects.
[expr for item in iterable if condition] builds a new list in one line.
Immutable ordered sequence written (a, b); it cannot be changed after creation.
An object whose hash value never changes, so it may be a dict key or set item; numbers, strings and tuples of hashables qualify.
A mapping of unique hashable keys to values, written {key: value}.
The error raised when a missing key is read with d[k]; d.get(k) returns None instead of failing.
Unordered collection of unique hashable items written {a, b}; supports |, &, - and <=.
Stack is LIFO via append() and pop(); queue is FIFO via append() and pop(0), and pop(0) costs O(n).
Search on a sorted list that checks the middle item and halves the remaining range each step; O(log₂ n).

takeaways: A string is a sequence, so every read works by index or slice, but no assignment ever changes the original object.
Formatting, splitting, stripping and joining are the four moves that convert between one string and many strings.
A list variable stores a reference, so assignment copies the reference and not the contents, which is the root of most aliasing bugs.
A list comprehension packs a loop, a filter and an expression into one readable line and returns a fresh list.
A tuple is the right choice when a group of values travels together and must not be changed.
Dictionary access, insertion, replacement and deletion all work by key, and all average O(1) time.
Sets answer questions about membership, duplicates and overlap faster than any list loop.
Choosing append with pop for a stack is cheap, but append with pop(0) for a queue is O(n) per removal.
Binary search is faster than linear search only when the list is already sorted and random access is available.
bank_note: Long answers here are judged on correct, runnable code plus a clear statement of what each data structure costs and why, so always show the operation, the sample output and the complexity in one place.

bank.q: Define a string in Python. Explain what immutable means for strings and show with code what happens when you try to assign to s[0].
outline: String is a sequence of Unicode characters written in quotes
Immutable: the object's value cannot change after creation
s[0] = 'X' raises TypeError
Only rebinding s = new_string changes the name
Methods like upper() return a new string, not an edited one

bank.q: Explain slicing with start, stop and step, including negative values. Trace the output of s = 'PYTHON' for s[1:4], s[-3:], s[::-1] and s[0:6:2].
outline: Slice stops before stop index
Step defaults to 1 and may be negative
Negative index counts from the end: -1 is last
Traces: 'YTH', 'HON', 'NOHTYP', 'PYO'
Out-of-range slice bounds are clipped, no error

bank.q: Compare the three ways of formatting text in Python: the % operator, str.format() and f-strings. Mention escape sequences and width/precision specifiers.
outline: % operator is the oldest style
str.format() uses positional or named braces
f-string evaluates expressions directly, readable and fast
Escape sequences \n, \t, \\ and raw strings with r
Format spec like :.2f for two decimals, :>10 for width

bank.q: Explain split(), strip() and join() with examples, including split() with no argument and join() on an empty separator.
outline: split() with no argument splits on runs of whitespace and drops empty strings
split(',') keeps empty fields
strip() removes both ends only, lstrip and rstrip are one-sided
join() needs all items to be strings, else TypeError
''.join(parts) glues with nothing in between

bank.q: Explain list mutability, aliasing and copying. Why does b = a not create a copy, and how do you copy a list properly?
outline: A name holds a reference to the list object
b = a binds both names to one object
Change through either name is visible through the other
Copying: a[:], list(a), a.copy()
Copies are shallow, inner mutable objects are still shared
Use copy.deepcopy for nested structures

bank.q: Explain dictionary literals and the four core operations: adding a key, accessing a value, replacing a value and removing a key. Include get(), del and KeyError.
outline: Literal written as {key: value, ...}
d[k] returns a value or raises KeyError
d[k] = v adds a new key or replaces the old value
del d[k] and d.pop(k) remove; pop returns the value
d.get(k, default) is the safe read
Keys must be unique and hashable, insertion order is kept

bank.q: Explain sets and the operations union, intersection, difference and subset test, with both operators and methods. Compare set with frozenset.
outline: Set holds unique hashable items, written with braces
a | b or a.union(b); a & b or a.intersection(b)
a - b or a.difference(b); a <= b subset test
Duplicates are collapsed automatically
frozenset is immutable, so it can be a dict key or an element of another set

bank.q: Write a Python program that reads a sentence, splits it into words, counts each word using a dictionary and prints the words in alphabetical order with their counts.
outline: Read with input() and lower() for uniformity
split() to get words, strip punctuation if required
Loop with counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1
sorted(counts) or sorted(counts.items()) for order
Loop to print word and count

bank.q: Write list comprehensions to (a) build the squares of even numbers from 1 to 20 and (b) flatten a 3 by 3 nested list into one list. Give the equivalent for-loop for each.
outline: Filter in the comprehension: [n*n for n in range(1,21) if n % 2 == 0]
Nested loops in one comprehension: [x for row in m for x in row]
Order of the for clauses decides the output order
Show the for-loop equivalent to prove equivalence
Mention that the comprehension creates a new list

bank.q: Write functions for push and pop on a list used as a stack, and for enqueue and dequeue used as a queue. Trace the output for a given sequence of calls and state the error raised on an empty pop.
outline: push uses lst.append(x), pop uses lst.pop()
enqueue uses lst.append(x), dequeue uses lst.pop(0)
Stack: LIFO, last pushed leaves first
Queue: FIFO, first added leaves first
Empty pop raises IndexError; guard with if lst

bank.q: Write Python functions for linear search and for binary search on a sorted list. For a sorted list of 15 items, give the maximum number of comparisons each makes for a key that is absent.
outline: Linear search compares every item, O(n), up to 15 comparisons
Binary search keeps low and high, compares middle
mid = (low + high) // 2, move low or high past mid
Maximum comparisons = ceil(log₂ 16) = 4
Binary search needs a sorted list; sorting first costs O(n log n)

bank.q: A student writes b = a, then b.append(4), and is surprised that a changed too. Analyse the cause, state what would have happened for strings and tuples, and give two correct ways to copy.
outline: Both names hold the same reference, one list object
Mutating through b is mutating through a
For an immutable string or tuple, b = a is safe because nothing can change in place
Fixes: b = a[:] and b = a.copy() or list(a)
Warn that all of these are shallow copies
Deep copy needed when inner items are themselves lists

bank.q: Evaluate the use of a Python list as a stack and as a queue. Compare the cost of pop() and pop(0), and recommend a structure for a busy queue.
outline: append is amortised O(1), pop from the end is O(1)
pop(0) shifts every remaining item, so it is O(n)
A queue built only on a list becomes O(n²) for n removals
collections.deque gives O(1) at both ends
List is fine for stacks and small queues, deque for high volume

bank.q: Design a small library system: books with a number of copies, a record of issued books, and search by title. Choose a list, tuple, dictionary or set for each part, and justify each choice in terms of the operations required.
outline: Dictionary book_title to copies for O(1) lookup and update
Set of issued book ids gives automatic uniqueness and fast membership
Tuple for fixed records such as (book_id, member_id, date)
List for an ordered history or shelf order
Search sorted titles with binary search, else dictionary lookup
State complexity of each chosen operation
Handle missing keys with get() or membership test

glossary.def: Text written inside single, double or triple quotes, for example 'hello'.
A backslash followed by a character that stands for a special character, such as \n for newline and \t for tab.
Joining two strings end to end with the + operator.
Repeating a string a given number of times with the * operator, as in 'ab' * 3 giving 'ababab'.
Any contiguous part of a string; in Python it is produced by slicing and never by editing.
Visiting each item of a sequence in turn, usually with for item in sequence.
A standard that assigns an integer code point to every character in every script.
A 7-bit character code for English letters, digits and symbols, now a small subset of Unicode.
The in operator; it tests substring for strings and item presence for lists, sets and dict keys.
A list whose items are themselves lists, used for tables and matrices and read as a[i][j].
The property of being changeable in place; lists, dicts and sets are mutable, strings and tuples are not.
Building a tuple by writing a, b = 1, 2 and pulling it apart again by the same syntax.
The live objects returned by keys(), values() and items(), which reflect later changes to the dict.
The set of items in either set, written a | b.
The set of items present in both sets, written a & b.
The items of one set that are not in another, written a - b.
A set is a subset of another when every one of its items lies in the other, written a <= b.
An immutable set, so it can itself be a dictionary key or an element of another set.
How the number of steps grows with input size n, written with big-O notation such as O(n) or O(log₂ n).
A built-in that returns a new sorted list from any iterable, leaving the original unchanged.
The key= function passed to sort or sorted to decide the ranking of each item.
Last in first out for a stack, first in first out for a queue, describing which item leaves first.
A string that reads the same forwards and backwards, easily tested with s == s[::-1].
